description:
AKA pumpkin pine

Eastern White Pines are sometimes called pumpkin pines because they develop a warm, orange color over time through a combination of quality wood and aging. 

To develop the pumpkin pine color, sawn boards are placed between layers of straw and turned and wiped down every two years. This process can take up to 70 years to complete.

"Pumpkin pine"  is often reclaimed from historic structures that have been demolished.


Eastern white pine needles exceed the amount of vitamin C of lemons and oranges[18] and make an excellent herbal tea. The cambium is edible. It is also a source of resveratrol. Linnaeus noted in the 18th century that cattle and pigs fed pine bark bread grew well, but he personally did not like the taste. Caterpillars of Lusk's pinemoth (Coloradia luski) have been found to feed only on Pinus strobus.

Pine tar is produced by slowly burning pine roots, branches, or small trunks in a partially smothered flame. Pine tar mixed with beer can be used to remove tapeworms (flat worms) or nematodes (round worms). Pine tar mixed with sulfur is useful to treat dandruff, and marketed in present-day products. Pine tar can also be processed to make turpentine.[19]

Native American traditional uses

The name "Adirondack" is an Iroquois word which means tree-eater and referred to their neighbors (more commonly known as the Algonquians) who collected the inner bark of this tree, Picea rubens, and others during times of winter starvation. The white soft inner bark (cambial layer) was carefully separated from the hard, dark brown bark and dried. When pounded this product can be used as flour or added to stretch other starchy products.[20][21]

The young staminate cones were stewed by the OjibweIndians with meat and were said to be sweet and not pitchy. In addition, the seeds are sweet and nutritious, but not as tasty as those of some of the western nut pines.[20]

Pine resin (sap) has been used by various tribes to waterproof baskets, pails, and boats. The Chippewa also used pine resin to successfully treat infections and even gangrenous wounds.[20] This is because pine resin apparently has a number of quite efficient antimicrobials. Generally a wet pulp from the inner bark, or pine tar mixed with beeswax or butter was applied to wounds and used as a salve to prevent infection.

Eastern White Pine
•	Annual or perennial: Perennial
•	Season: Cones are produced between May and June.
•	Description: A very common pine tree, easily denoted by the number of needles per cluster, which is five. Other pines have different numbers per cluster—Red Pines have two, and Pitch Pines have three, for example. Also have longer, thinner cones than other pines. Needles are slender and two to five inches long.
•	Habitat: A dominant tree in mixed forests. Prefers sandy soils in moist areas, but can survive in swamp or highland habitats.
•	Predator/Parasitism: The White Pine Cone Beetle preys on cones, laying eggs inside that will feed on seeds from the time they hatch until they reach maturity.

description: These pictures of the eastern white pine and it’s pinecones were taken where my backyard meets the barrier of the US Route 22. This pine tree was amongst many other different plants gathered in very close proximity near the highway. As I was walking around my backyard, I noticed these three pinecones being some of the few left hanging on the tree, and decided to take a picture of them. When these pictures were taken, it was a cloudy day with a slight chance of rain. It was also very hot and humid, with temperatures around 82°F, but the real feel at around 88°F. There was also wind that came and went periodically, but it wasn’t difficult to take a picture of the pinecones because they seemed to weigh the branch down a little. As you can see from the pictures, some of the needles on this eastern white pine tree have become yellow, or even brown; however, after doing some research about why this may happen, I have found that because the yellowing of the needles seems to occur only on the inner portions of the branches, it is a natural process that will only last a short while.

description:
Osage Mountain, Bartram Trail, North Carolina

I *do* check the weather report before I go on a hike, and it said nothing of hurricane force winds or anything like. However, as I commenced my hike, the winds began picking up a bit. And by the time I reached the goal of the hike, a rocky bald, the winds had increased volubly. As I stood on the lee side of the mountain taking this photo, the winds increased in ferocity, their passage through the tree tops creating a roar like a jet revving its engines for take off. I was fatigued from the climb to the bald, but intended rest and repast were forsaken for an immediate and hasty descent, the winds roaring away overhead. By and by I hit the trail and returned to the car without mishap. No  wind felled trees lay in the path nor across the road, much to my relief. When I arrived back home, there were no winds to speak of, and none were reported by my family. Perhaps a peculiar dip in the jet stream had descended upon the mountain? I dunno. That partially sums up my experience whilst snapping these photos atop Osage Mountain.
